statement: Half of Ana's marbles is the same number as one third of Bo's marbles. Together they have 40 marbles. How many marbles does Bo have?

choices.misconception: I found the size of one equal part, $40 \div 5 = 8$, and stopped there.
I worked out how many marbles Ana has instead of Bo.
I thought half and a third being equal meant they have the same number, so I split 40 in half.
I thought Bo has three times as many as Ana, so I split 40 into 4 parts and took 3 of them.

hints: Call the equal amount one block.
If half of Ana's marbles is one block, Ana has two blocks. If a third of Bo's is one block, Bo has three blocks. Draw the blocks and use the total.
Ana has 2 blocks and Bo has 3 blocks, so 5 equal blocks make 40 marbles.

solutions.reliable: Let one block be the number that is half of Ana's marbles and also a third of Bo's. Then Ana has 2 blocks and Bo has 3 blocks, 5 blocks in all. Since 5 blocks make 40, one block is 8. Bo has $3 \times 8 = 24$. Check: Ana has 16, half of 16 is 8, and a third of 24 is 8. The transferable idea: turn "a fraction of one equals a fraction of another" into equal blocks.
solutions.elegant: Try the choices: if Bo has 24, Ana has 16, and half of 16 equals a third of 24, both 8. No other choice works, so the bar model and back-solving agree.

whyOnTest: Turning a statement about equal fractions into equal blocks is the bar-model idea behind many harder sharing problems.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
